newsitem.title: ECUADOR: IMF experts said to oppose Ecuador convertibility.
newsitem.headline: IMF experts said to oppose Ecuador convertibility.

text.p: Some International Monetary Fund officials in Ecuador oppose it adopting currency "convertibility," which they see as a currency straightjacket, a senior Ecuadorean government official said Tuesday.
"It isn't the International Monetary Fund as an institution which opposes convertibility. It is some of its officials who are in the country," the official told Reuters.
IMF officials arrived in Ecuador last month to review its macroeconomic performance.
The official said some of them fear convertibility would make it "impossible to solve the economic effects of an external crisis, such as the conflict with Peru in 1995."
Ecuador and Peru fought a brief jungle border war in early 1995 which knocked Ecuador's economy off course and resulted in currency devaluation, new taxes and higher interest rates.

Finance Minister Pablo Concha said Monday Ecuador will take on convertibility as part of an economic plan to be announced in a few days. Concha has not revealed full details of the planned convertibility but says the sucre would be pegged at no more than 4,000 to the dollar.
Around noon Tuesday the dollar was trading at about 3,398 sucres.

Ecuador's populist new President Abdala Bucaram has taken on former Argentine Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo as an adviser. Cavallo introduced convertibility to Argentina, pegging the peso at par to the dollar in 1991 with major benefits for the Argentine economy.

But the government official said it was Bucaram rather than Cavallo who proposed convertibility for Ecuador. "It was the president who did it, then hired Cavallo. The former Argentine minister has even said Ecuador is not in the right shape to do so," said the official, asking not to be named.

Bucaram's government had been due to announce its economic program this Sunday after talks in the resort of Salinas south of Quito. But the Secretary General of the Administration, Miguel Salem, said this timetable might be delayed.

"If we finish Saturday it will be Sunday 24; if we finish Sunday it will be Monday," he said. Doubts about the economic program caused nervousness in the local market and the Central Bank had to intervene Tuesday against dollar-buying.
